text: On the forehand drive, keep a gap between your elbow and your ribs. A tucked elbow makes the stroke short and weak.
Feel your weight move from the back foot to the front foot during the forehand. If it stays on one foot, the arm does all the work.
Contact the forehand slightly in front of your body. Behind you, the bat can only go sideways.
Keep the wrist quiet on the forehand drive. Wrist flicks add errors faster than they add speed.
A deep forehand is harder to attack than a fast one. Aim for the last third of the table.
On the backhand, let your thumb press lightly on the blade. It helps you feel the angle.
The backhand drive is short. If your bat finishes behind your shoulder, the stroke is too big.
Most backhand errors are angle errors, not effort errors. Fix the bat angle before you swing harder.
From a backhand rally, the line to their forehand is the surprise ball. Use it when they lean to their backhand.
Every push is a choice: short to stop the attack, or long and fast to rush them. A half-long push is the worst of both.
Push with real backspin. A floaty push is an invitation to loop.
Change between heavy and light pushes with the same look. Opponents loop light pushes long and heavy pushes into the net.
A long push wide to the backhand pulls a right-handed player off the table. Then their forehand corner is open.
Against backspin, the bat starts below the ball. You can't lift what you are already above.
Spin comes from a thin contact: brush the ball, don't push it.
Beginner loopers hit too early. Against backspin, wait for the ball to start dropping: it gives you time and spin.
The second loop is harder than the first. Recover the moment you finish the first one.
Against a block, swing more forward and close the bat. The ball already has topspin, so it doesn't need lifting.
Loop the first attack into the playing elbow. It forces a decision and often a weak block.
Counter-looping starts with your feet: step back first, then you have time to swing.
Counter-loop over the top of the ball. Underneath it, their spin sends your ball long.
The backhand topspin needs a loose wrist. Cock it back, then let it snap through the ball.
Keep the backhand elbow in front of your body. It is the hinge the whole stroke turns on.
Block early, on the rise. The longer you wait, the more the spin takes over.
A soft grip on the block kills the pace: the ball dies short over the net. A firm grip sends it back fast.
Blocking wins with angles, not power. Move the looper from corner to corner.
If your block has a backswing, it's not a block. Bat in front, small push, done.
Flicks start with the foot. Step in under the table first, then the bat is close enough to the ball.
Flick to the corners or the elbow, not to the middle of the table where they wait.
The banana flick brushes around the side of the ball. It handles heavier backspin more safely than a straight flick.
To keep a ball short, touch it early, right after the bounce, with almost no swing.
A short ball to the forehand is awkward for most players. Use it when you need to stop an attack.
Smash at the top of the bounce. Too early and the ball is still rising; too late and it is below the net.
Smash wide, not at the lobber. A second smash in the same spot comes back.
Against a good lob, the first smash doesn't need to win. Keep it deep and wait for a shorter lob.
A lob that lands deep with topspin kicks away. A short lob is a gift.
Add a little sidespin to your lob: it curves and is harder to smash cleanly.
Chop as the ball drops beside you. Chopping it early makes it pop up.
A chopper's best weapon is variation: heavy, then light with the same look.
Choppers move more than anyone. Big side steps, then back to the middle.
A chopper who never attacks is easy to play. Look for the one loose ball and hit it.
Penholders: keep the fingers on the back relaxed. Tight fingers lock the wrist.
Check your grip now and then. Grips drift during a session, usually toward the forehand.
Bat at table height between shots. From there it can go up, down, left or right equally fast.
Stand about an arm's length from the table. Too close and you get jammed; too far and short balls beat you.
Two minutes of ball bouncing on the bat each day builds feel faster than you'd think.
Try bouncing the ball on the edge of the bat, then the face. Silly, but it sharpens your touch.
Aim 10 cm higher over the net in practice than you think you need. Most misses are in the net.
Count your rallies out loud. Counting turns a drill into a small game and keeps you focused.
When a serve goes long, step back half a step before you attack. It gives the ball time to come to you.
Attack a long backspin serve with lift; attack a long topspin serve with a forward swing.
Watch the server's bat, not their face or body. The contact tells you the spin.
Backspin floats and slows or checks after the bounce; topspin dips in the air and kicks forward after the bounce.
A big arm swing with a soft contact usually means little spin. Many 'heavy' serves are actually no-spin.
If you can't read it, play a safe, controlled return rather than a big attack.
On receive, keep it low before you keep it fast. A high return is attacked whatever its speed.
Stand so you can reach a short ball to your forehand and a long ball to your backhand. Usually a little to the backhand side, close.
Don't receive the same way every time. Mix short, long and flick so the server can't plan the third ball.
Want a better backhand? Fix your feet first. Most backhand misses come from a ball beside the body.
